known_facts_book1: Cries 'It is the voice of my child! My precious Lily! My imperial kitten!' and knocks the White King over among the cinders rushing past him.
Is carried onto the table by Alice, and loses her breath from the rapid journey through the air.
Comes running through the wood after the crow with both arms stretched out as if she were flying, and loses her shawl.
Is dreadfully untidy: every single thing crooked, all over pins, the brush entangled in her hair, and the comb lost yesterday.
Offers Alice a lady's-maid place at twopence a week and jam every other day, the rule being jam to-morrow and jam yesterday but never jam to-day.
Lives backwards, so that her memory works both ways, and remembers best the things that happened the week after next.
Cites the King's Messenger, who is in prison being punished before his trial next Wednesday, the crime coming last of all.
Screams before she pricks her finger on the shawl brooch, and does not scream at all once she has pricked it.
Says she is just one hundred and one, five months and a day, and that she has sometimes believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast.
Turns into an old Sheep knitting behind a shop counter, her last 'better' ending in a long bleat.
Tells Alice she can read words of one letter.
Asks the examination questions about Division and the cause of lightning, and tells the story of the thunderstorm that left her unable to remember her own name.
Says Humpty Dumpty came to the door with a corkscrew in his hand looking for a hippopotamus.
Falls asleep on Alice's shoulder, and at the banquet recites the riddle in poetry about the fish and the dish-cover.
Disappears into the soup tureen, her face grinning at Alice for a moment over the edge, with a leg of mutton left sitting in her chair.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Whose Pawn Alice becomes; Alice straightens her shawl and hair and carries her asleep.
known_relations_book1.White King: Her King, whom she knocks over among the cinders and who worries about her running speed.
known_relations_book1.Red Queen: Her fellow Queen at the examination and the banquet, who apologises for her and calls her good-tempered.
known_relations_book1.Sheep: What she turns into at the end of the wool-and-water chapter.
known_relations_book1.Snowdrop: The white kitten Alice decides she was.

the White Queen is Alice's mother

the White Queen presides over a trial

known_facts_book1: Is knocked among the cinders by the White Queen and comes up covered with ashes from head to foot.
Can neither hear nor see Alice, and is astonished to find himself held in the air by an invisible hand and dusted.
Says he turned cold to the very ends of his whiskers, and is told by the Queen that he hasn't got any whiskers.
Writes in an enormous memorandum-book, and asks for a thinner pencil when Alice writes for him.
Has sent four thousand two hundred and seven soldiers and horses, keeping back two horses wanted in the game.
Keeps two Messengers, Haigha and Hatta, one to come and one to go, one to fetch and one to carry.
Makes the joke about Nobody on the road walking slower than the Messenger.
Says the crown the Lion and the Unicorn are fighting for is his all the while.
Threatens to have Hatta buttered for shouting a whisper that went through his head like an earthquake.
Says of the White Queen that you might as well try to catch a Bandersnatch, and makes a memorandum about her instead of helping.
Gave Humpty Dumpty his cravat as an un-birthday present, together with the White Queen, and promised him all his horses and all his men.

known_relations_book1.White Queen: His Queen, who knocks him into the cinders and whom he declines to run after.
known_relations_book1.Alice: Cannot see or hear her in the first chapter; talks with her freely from the seventh onward.
known_relations_book1.Haigha: One of his two Anglo-Saxon Messengers, who carries his ham sandwiches and hay.
known_relations_book1.Hatta: His other Messenger, just out of prison, whom he threatens to have buttered.
known_relations_book1.Humpty Dumpty: Gave him the cravat and the promise of all his horses and all his men.
